VJ software compared

VDMX vs Resolume: which VJ software is right for you?

By Syd Lawrence, a visual artist and developer who makes Vibresia. Facts last checked 2 November 2026; updated 2 November 2026.

If you play shows on Windows as well as a Mac, or you want the software many venues already run, pick Resolume: Avenue is €299 and Arena adds media-server features for €799. If you work only on a Mac and want a modular rig you wire up yourself, with MIDI, OSC and DMX control and audio analysis, pick VDMX, from US$199.99. Both are one-time purchases, and both let you try the full app before you pay.

Pick Resolume if

you play on both macOS and Windows, you want the tool a lot of venues and VJs already know, or you need media-server features, which come with Arena at €799. Avenue at €299 covers VJing on its own.

Pick VDMX if

you work only on a Mac and like building your own setup: layers, FX chains, MIDI, OSC and DMX control, audio analysis, LFOs and step sequencers. It starts at US$199.99, and US$349 adds Vuo and TouchDesigner integration.

Where Resolume wins

It runs on Windows as well as macOS. Resolume is listed for Mac, Windows. If your show laptop is a PC, or you swap between machines at different venues, that settles it. VDMX is for Mac only.

It's the common choice. It is an industry-standard pair: Avenue for VJing, Arena adding media-server features. Its stated audience is working VJs and venues running video on screens and projectors. Picking the tool a venue already uses can make a handover or a shared booth easier.

Clear tiers for different jobs. Avenue (€299) is the VJ app. Arena (€799) adds media-server features for bigger rooms. Wire (€399) is a separate visual programming tool, for building your own effects and generators. Each licence includes 12 months of updates, and the licence keeps working once those 12 months are up.

Where VDMX wins

A lower starting price. VDMX's main licence, VDMX6, is US$199.99, one-time. Vidvox also mentions educational, hobbyist and upgrade discounts, though it doesn't list the amounts.

A modular rig you build yourself. It does layer compositing with blend modes, masks and real-time FX chains. Control comes from MIDI, OSC and DMX, and it can drive parameters from audio analysis, LFOs and step sequencers. That suits people who want to design how their show behaves rather than use a fixed layout.

Open formats and links to other software. It runs ISF (GLSL) generators and effects alongside FFGL and Vuo. It takes video in and sends it out over Syphon and NDI, drives fullscreen displays, and records to disk. VDMX6 Plus, at US$349, adds Vuo and TouchDesigner integration. TouchDesigner itself is licensed separately.

One caution on this section: the control and I/O details here come from VDMX's own page, and our record of Resolume doesn't cover its control options or video connections. Resolume has its own, so if MIDI, OSC, Syphon, Spout or NDI decide it for you, check Resolume's site before you choose.

A trial without a watermark. The VDMX trial is fully functional except that you can't save projects. You can judge the output exactly as an audience would see it.

Where both fall short

Neither is free. Both are paid, one-time purchases, and neither has a free tier. Expect to spend US$199.99 at the low end for VDMX and €299 for Resolume.

Both trials hold something back. Resolume is free to use for as long as you like, but its video output carries a Resolume watermark and its audio has a robot voice until you enter a serial number. That's fine for practice and not for a paying show. VDMX's trial won't save projects, so you can't build a set over several days and keep it without buying.

The extras cost extra. On Resolume, media-server features mean Arena rather than Avenue, and Wire is a separate purchase. On VDMX, Vuo and TouchDesigner integration means the Plus licence, and TouchDesigner needs its own licence on top.

What it costs

Prices are as listed on each shop, in the currency each one sells in. We haven't converted them, because the price you pay depends on your own bank's rate and any local tax.

A Mac-only VJ wanting the basic app: Resolume Avenue is €299; VDMX6 is US$199.99. A VJ wanting more: Resolume Arena is €799, and VDMX6 Plus is US$349. Those two upgrades add different things, media-server features on one and Vuo and TouchDesigner integration on the other, so compare what you need rather than the totals. Every Resolume licence includes 12 months of updates and keeps working after them.

Questions people ask

Is VDMX cheaper than Resolume?

At the entry level, VDMX6 is US$199.99 and Resolume Avenue is €299. They're priced in different currencies, so check the rate on the day you buy.

Does VDMX run on Windows?

No. VDMX needs macOS 13 or later, Intel or Apple silicon. Resolume runs on Mac, Windows.

Can I try Resolume and VDMX for free?

Yes, both. Free to use indefinitely, but video output has a Resolume watermark and audio has a robot voice until a serial number is entered. The VDMX trial is fully functional except saving projects.

Do Resolume licences stop working after a year?

No. Each licence includes 12 months of updates, and it keeps working after those 12 months end.
